summary: Specifies conventions for using the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including algorithm identifier and public key syntax. The algorithm itself is described in RFC 8554. It obsoletes RFC 8708.

eli5.summary: Some signatures rely only on hash fingerprints, which are believed to stay safe even against future super-powerful computers. This explains using them in signed messages. It replaces RFC 8708.

subtitle: How to sign CMS messages with hash-based HSS/LMS signatures that are considered safe against quantum computers.

tldr.problem: Widely used signature algorithms such as RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA are vulnerable if cryptographically relevant quantum computers are ever built, so a quantum-safe option is needed for signed messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm from RFC 8554 is used in CMS: an object identifier, an OCTET STRING signature and public key format, and rules for the SignerInfo fields.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8708, adds newly defined tree sizes and LM-OTS signatures, and aligns the public key definition with use in X.509 certificates.

today: RFC 9708 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025. It obsoletes RFC 8708 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 9708 specifies the conventions for using the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) / Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) hash-based signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) signed-data content type. The algorithm itself is described in RFC 8554. The RFC also provides the algorithm identifier and the public key syntax.

The motivation is the future threat from quantum computers. If cryptographically relevant quantum computers are ever built, RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA would all be vulnerable. HSS/LMS does not rely on discrete logarithms or factoring. It relies on a second-preimage-resistant hash function, so it is considered post-quantum secure. One use the RFC names is protecting software updates.

The algorithm has trade-offs. It can only be used for a fixed number of signing operations with a given private key. Public keys are small and the computational cost is low, but signatures are quite large. Parameter sets are currently defined that use SHA-256 and SHAKE256.
sections.eli5: Future super-computers might crack some of today's signature locks. Signatures made from fingerprints of data should still hold up, but each key can only sign a limited number of times and the signatures are big.

sections.title: The HSS/LMS Algorithm in Brief
sections.content:
The Merkle Tree Signature (MTS) scheme signs a large but fixed number of messages. It depends on a one-time signature method and a collision-resistant hash function. RFC 8554 uses the Leighton and Micali adaptation of the Lamport-Diffie-Winternitz-Merkle one-time signature system.

The hierarchy has three layers. HSS is a hierarchy of trees: the signer can generate subordinate trees when needed, because generating one whole tree might take weeks or longer. Each tree uses LMS, and each leaf of an LMS tree is tied to a LM-OTS one-time signature. In an HSS signature, the private key of a parent tree signs the public key of a child tree, and the bottom-most tree signs the actual message.

An LMS tree of height h has 2^h leaves. RFC 8554 supports h=5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, with SHA-256 and m=32 bytes of hash output. LM-OTS has the parameters n, H, w, p and ls, and RFC 8554 supports w=1, 2, 4 and 8. Further parameter sets are registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: Imagine a big tree where every leaf is a pen that can write exactly one signature. Trees can hang under other trees, and each parent vouches for its children, so you only build the branches you need.

sections.title: Signature and Key Layout
sections.content:
An HSS signature starts with u32str(Nspk), the number of signed public keys, followed by that many signed public keys, and then the LMS signature over the message. For a standalone tree, Nspk is zero. Nspk is the number of levels in the hierarchy minus 1.

An LMS signature has four elements: the leaf number q, an LM-OTS signature value, a typecode for the LMS algorithm, and an authentication path. The path holds the siblings of the nodes from the leaf up to the root, so a tree of height h has h values. An LM-OTS signature is the variant identifier, a random n-byte value C, and the hash values y[0] through y[p-1].

The LMS public key is u32str(lms_algorithm_type) || u32str(otstype) || I || T[1]. An HSS public key outside a certificate is an OCTET STRING with the number of levels L followed by the LMS public key. When L=1, the HSS system is a single tree.
sections.eli5: A signature is a receipt that says which leaf was used, shows the one-time pen's mark, and lists the neighbouring branches so anyone can walk back up to the top of the tree and check it.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Public Keys
sections.content:
The algorithm identifier is id-alg-hss-lms-hashsig, the object identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.3.17. The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be absent, which means not present at all and not set to NULL. The same identifier is also referred to as id-alg-mts-hashsig, a name from an early draft of RFC 8554.

In CMS the HSS/LMS signature value is a large OCTET STRING. It is designed for easy parsing: the HSS, LMS and LM-OTS parts each carry a counter and a typecode that give everything needed to parse the value during validation. The signature value identifies the hash function used in the tree.

When the identifier appears in the SubjectPublicKeyInfo of an X.509 certificate, the key usage extension is constrained. A CA certificate MUST contain at least one of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign and cRLSign, and no other values. An end-entity certificate MUST contain at least one of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation or cRLSign, and no other values.
sections.eli5: The algorithm has a name tag, a long number, that says what kind of signature it is. The tag carries no extras, and certificates may only list a few allowed jobs for the key.

sections.title: Signed-Data Conventions
sections.content:
CMS computes the signature differently depending on whether signed attributes are present. If they are absent, HSS/LMS signs the content directly. If they are present, a hash of the content is computed with the same hash function used in the HSS/LMS tree, a message-digest attribute holds it, and the HSS/LMS signature is computed over the DER-encoded set of signed attributes. That set MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute.

The SignerInfo fields are used as follows:

  • digestAlgorithm MUST contain the one-way hash function used in the HSS/LMS tree. The RFC repeats the identifiers for SHA-256 and SHAKE256.
  • signatureAlgorithm MUST contain id-alg-hss-lms-hashsig, with the parameters field absent.
  • signature contains the single HSS/LMS signature value produced by the signing operation in RFC 8554.
sections.eli5: When you sign a letter, you either sign the letter itself, or you write a fingerprint of it on a cover sheet and sign the cover sheet. Either way the same fingerprint maker used by the tree must be used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST protect private keys, because compromise lets an attacker forge signatures. They MUST also keep track of which leaf nodes have been used. Losing the integrity of that tracking data can make a one-time key get used more than once. The RFC warns that failed writes, virtual machine snapshotting or cloning, and other operational concerns must be considered when the key and tracking data live on non-volatile media or in a virtual machine.

An implementation MUST generate each LMS key pair independently of all others in the HSS tree. It MUST ensure that an LM-OTS private key generates a signature only one time and is not used for anything else.

Private key generation relies on random numbers, and a weak pseudorandom number generator can leave little or no security. Signature generation also uses random numbers, with much less severe consequences, but the guidance in RFC 4086 still matters. When computing signatures, the same hash function SHOULD be used for the message digest of the content and of the signed attributes, if present.
sections.eli5: Each one-time pen must never be used twice, so keep a careful list of used pens and guard the pen box. Make the pens from truly random choices, not guessable ones.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 8708
sections.content:
When RFC 8708 was published, no one planned to put an HSS/LMS public key in a certificate. Now there are plans to do so, so the pk-HSS-LMS-HashSig definition was updated to show no ASN.1 wrapping of the public key. This resolves errata 7960 and 7963. The KEY field does not matter inside CMS, but it needs to be consistent with how a key is carried in a certificate.

Newer tree sizes and LM-OTS signature types that have been defined since are now listed, and Section 4 gives more detail on the allowed X.509 key usage values. The IANA registry references for value 64 in the S/MIME module identifier registry and value 17 in the S/MIME algorithms registry now point to this document.
sections.eli5: This is a corrected edition. It fixes how the public key is written down, adds new tree sizes, and spells out more clearly what a key may be used for.

root.label: Top LMS tree
root.note: Its public key is the HSS public key

children.label: Child LMS tree
children.note: Its public key is signed by the parent tree
